common_name: Ebony Echeveria (Near-Black Wax Agave Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Grow in bright light to full sun in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; the near-black leaf color deepens with strong light and cooler nights and fades toward green in shade.

directions: This selected form of the wax agave echeveria keeps the same thick, geometric, pointed leaves as the straight species but saturates them to a deep purple-black across nearly the whole leaf rather than just the tips. Plant in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix and set rosettes where they get several hours of direct sun, since low light causes the dark pigment to fade and the rosette to stretch loosely. Water only after the soil has dried out completely, keeping moisture off the leaves and out of the rosette center to prevent rot. Established plants send up arching stalks of small coral-and-yellow bell flowers in spring, and offsets can be detached and rooted to start new plants.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in bright light to full sun in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; give it the coolest nights and brightest light possible for the darkest leaf color.

directions: Native to central Mexico, Echeveria affinis is a true species rather than a hybrid, forming a loose, slightly open rosette of narrow, tapering leaves that darken to an intense blackish-green to near-black under bright, cool conditions, making it one of the darkest species echeverias grown rather than a bred hybrid like the many black-leaved cultivars already in cultivation. It is also one of the parent species behind several popular near-black hybrid echeverias. Plant in sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun and let it dry out completely between waterings, since the thinner leaves are more prone to rot than thicker-leaved relatives if kept damp. Older rosettes develop a short visible stem and send up red-orange bell flowers on arching stalks in winter to early spring.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: False Liveforever Echeveria (Mat-Forming Blue-Green Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Set rooted offsets into fast-draining succulent mix in spring, spacing them to allow the creeping stolons room to spread into a colony.

directions: Native to the mountains of Nuevo Leon, Mexico, Echeveria simulans stands apart from most of its relatives by spreading through underground stolons, so a single plant slowly forms a loose colony of small, tight, blue-green rosettes instead of staying as one solitary clump. The compact, spoon-shaped leaves carry maroon-red tips that intensify in bright sun and cool weather, echoing the coloring of other echeverias in this collection but on a distinctly mat-forming, ground-hugging plant. Grow it in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, watering only once the mix is fully dry, and give it room to roam since new rosettes will keep popping up beyond the original planting spot. Short stalks of small yellow-orange bell flowers appear in late spring to summer above the foliage.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
